t0_3.what:
These three special files handle a route's error/loading states — without a single line of state management.

loading.tsx added shows a skeleton until the data arrives; error.tsx added shows a graceful message + retry when a crash occurs.
t0_3.analogy: Restaurant — as soon as you place an order, the starter arrives (loading.tsx). If the dish goes wrong, the manager comes with an apology and serves a fresh order (error.tsx). Items not on the menu get a “not available” card (not-found.tsx).
t0_3.why: Server components are async — data takes time to arrive, and it can fail somewhere. Without these files, each page would need its own loading/error state. Next has created a convention for this.
pros: Zero boilerplate — add the file, no state management needed.
Error isolation — a single widget fails, not the whole page.
Retry with reset() without a reload.
cons: error.tsx must be a client component.
In production, error.message is redacted — debugging requires a separate approach.
In nested routes, you have to track which boundary will catch it.
gotchas: In error.tsx you must include 'use client' — otherwise you get a build error.
Error bubbles upward — the nearest parent error.tsx catches it, not the one that threw it.
global-error.tsx replaces the root layout — you have to write <html><body> yourself.
terms: The immediate fallback for a route until its data arrives — a Suspense boundary is created automatically.
Fallback when rendering fails — ErrorBoundary + reset() retry button.
The 404 UI shown when notFound() is called or the URL is invalid.
where: Skeletons for slow queries — the page doesn’t appear white.
Retry UX via error.tsx without an extra library.
Invalid ID triggers notFound() — proper 404 with SEO.
t0_3.visualCap: As soon as the request arrives, the fallback streams immediately; when the data arrives, it replaces it with the actual content.

t0_1.what:
layout.tsx wraps all its child pages and stays alive during navigation — the sidebar does not re-render, its state remains.

template.tsx does exactly the same work, but a new instance is created on each navigation.
t0_1.analogy: Office building — walls, elevator, lobby (layout) never change; the furniture inside the rooms (template) changes with each tenant.
t0_1.why: Earlier the entire page re-rendered on every navigation — the sidebar flickered, scroll position was lost. Layouts provided a persistent shell: only the inner part changes.
pros: State preserved — filled inputs, scroll position, video playback all remain.
Complex shells can be built with nested layouts without prop drilling.
You can fetch data in a layout and pass it to children.
cons: A layout never unloads — if it holds incorrect state, the entire app is affected.
The difference between template and layout is confusing at first.
If the root layout lacks html/body, the build fails.
gotchas: Writing <html> and <body> tags in the root layout is ESSENTIAL — otherwise you get a hydration error.
useState inside a layout does NOT reset on navigation — this is a feature, not a bug.
useEffect in templates runs again on every navigation — sometimes this is exactly what you need.
terms: The surrounding framework that stays the same across navigation — state is preserved, no re-render.
Similar to a layout, but a new mount occurs on each navigation — previous state is discarded.
app/layout.tsx — essential; this is where the <html> and <body> tags are written.
where: Auth state, cart count — these reside in layouts so they don’t disappear on navigation.
Dashboard’s own sidebar, blog’s own header — from nested layouts.
Need a page-enter animation on every navigation? Not a layout, template.tsx.
t0_1.visualCap: On navigation, the layout stays in place while only the children change. If it were a template, the whole thing would remount.

The [slug] folder name is replaced in the URL by any value. app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx — /blog/react, /blog/css both work this way.

t0_2.analogy: A speed-post address label — the pattern stays the same, only the name-street (slug) is written differently on each envelope. One label format, hundreds of thousands of addresses.
t0_2.why: 1000 blog posts, 1000 folders? No. One dynamic route + a database = all posts from a single file. Think of it like REST’s :id, but in folders.

Very fast when combined with static generation.
Catch-all provides flexible URL structures.

t0_0.what:
In Next.js routing is created from folders. When you write app/users/page.tsx, the /users URL is generated automatically.

No route config, no react-router — the folder name is the URL.
t0_0.analogy: House rooms — a nameplate is placed on the door. Plate = folder name (URL), room contents = page.tsx. Seeing the nameplate, a guest goes directly to the room.
t0_0.why: Earlier each project had its own routing config — each with a different style. File-based routing introduced a convention: all projects have the same structure, so a new developer instantly understands where each page is.
pros: Zero config — create a folder, route ready.
The structure alone reveals the entire site.
Private files (_folder) and tools like groups are built-in.
cons: The folder name is the URL — renaming means changing URLs.
Deep nesting makes paths long.
New developers get stuck on “why doesn’t the components folder create a route?”

Folders inside the app/ directory become routes — no separate routing config is needed.
What will be displayed at that URL — without this file the folder does not become a route.
where: Pages, blogs, dashboards — everything is built with this.
You can keep component files inside a route folder — they do not become routes.
The first difference between "App Router vs Pages Router" is this — config vs convention.

t0_4.what:
In Next.js, to write SEO tags just export a metadata object — the framework puts it into the <head>.

For dynamic pages, use a generateMetadata() function — fetch the required data and return the title/description based on it.
t0_4.analogy: A book’s cover page — it doesn’t contain the interior content, but it’s the first thing you see before picking it up from the shelf. Metadata = the cover of your page, in search results and chat previews.
t0_4.why: Earlier you had to write <Head> components manually on every page — tags were duplicated or missed. The Metadata API turned this into a single export statement, and duplicate tags merged automatically.
pros: Declarative — no chance of forgetting to write tags.
Parent-child metadata merges automatically.
ImageResponse generates OG images from code.
cons: Works only in Server Components.
Running generateMetadata on every request adds database load.
OG image generation can take build time.
gotchas: You cannot export metadata from a client component ('use client') — results in a build error.
If both generateMetadata and the page fetch the same data, Request Memoization deduplicates it — avoid double fetching.

Dynamic metadata — each page’s own title based on its URL/data.

openGraph creates a nice preview card on WhatsApp/Twitter.

(marketing)/about/page.tsx and (shop)/cart/page.tsx — both different teams/different layouts, but the parentheses disappear in the URL: /about, /cart.

t0_5.why: In large apps there were two problems: (1) organizing pages with different layouts, (2) keeping something like a modal in sync with the URL. Groups provided organization, parallel routes gave a clean way for URL-driven modals.

Slots can load or error independently (their own loading.tsx).

t1_0.what:
Server Components can be async. Inside the component do a direct await — the data arrives before the HTML is generated.

The client-side cycle of useEffect + useState + loading spinner is eliminated.
t1_0.analogy: The kitchen chef goes to the market, brings the vegetables, then cooks the meal — the plate (HTML) is served only when the food is ready. The waiter (useEffect) doesn’t run back and forth in between.
t1_0.why: The client-side fetching flow was: empty page → JS load → effect runs → spinner → data arrives → render. The user saw a blank screen again. In RSC the data comes on the server — the first HTML is complete.
pros: Data is in the initial HTML — the spinner phase is gone.
Secrets stay safe on the server.
Running close to the database reduces latency.
cons: The component can block entirely until data arrives — Suspense is required.
For interactivity you still need a Client Component.
Libraries other than fetch (e.g., axios) don’t get caching options.
gotchas: Sequential awaits = waterfall — independent calls should always be in Promise.all. A favorite interview question.
This only extends to fetch — Prisma/axios don’t get memoization or cache options (React cache() is separate).
Browser APIs (window, localStorage) don’t work in a server component — they are client-only.
terms: Direct await fetch(...) inside a server component — no need for useEffect.
Next.js patches the native fetch — provides cache/revalidate options.
One fetch finishes, then the next starts — total time accumulates.
where: Product detail, blog post, profile — all use RSC fetch.
Secret keys stay on the server — they don’t go into the client bundle.
Prisma/Drisko direct await — fetch isn’t required either.
t1_0.visualCap: Sequential await = waterfall (adds up). Give independent fetches to Promise.all — they run together.

t1_1.what:
Layout, page, and 3 components — all calling getUser()? Only one request will go over the network. The rest will receive the same response.

This is React's cache() API that Next automatically applied to fetch.
t1_1.analogy: In a family, 5 people ordered the same pizza — the restaurant made ONE pizza and gave slices to everyone. Order (network call) once, food (data) for all.
t1_1.why: Nested layouts need the same data at multiple levels. Sending props down everywhere isn’t possible. Memoization eliminated the "props drilling or duplicate fetch" dilemma — fetch directly everywhere, the framework will dedupe.
pros: Code simple — fetch directly everywhere, optimization handled by the framework.
Props drilling eliminated.
Per-request scope — data does not leak between users.
cons: Only GET fetches are auto-deduped — POST or POST-like calls are not.
Memoization clears as soon as the request finishes — there is no persistent cache.
Different URLs/headers produce different cache keys, so deduplication won’t occur.
gotchas: Memoization is limited to a single request — the next visitor will fetch again. For persistence, look at Data Cache.
cache() works only on the server — not in client components.
Fetches that read cookies/headers are not deduped — each call is unique.
terms: During a single render, the same URL fetch occurs only once — the rest comes from cache.
React API to memoize functions per request — for calls outside fetch.
The entire render tree for an HTTP request — memoization lives only during this period.
where: Header + page + sidebar all need the user — three fetches, one network call.
Wrap cache() around Prisma calls to dedupe them as well.
"How to share the same data across multiple components?" – a modern interview answer.
t1_1.visualCap: A render tree, the same fetch in four places — only one request went over the network.

t1_2.what:
Data Cache is a cache that lives longer than a build/deploy. Data fetched for one user will be served to subsequent visitors as cached (until it is revalidated).

Control: fetch(url, { next: { revalidate: 60 } }) — cached for 60 seconds.
t1_2.analogy: Fridge — you don’t go to the market (origin server) every time. Bring groceries once, use the fridge. Set an alarm every hour (revalidate) to check for fresh milk.
t1_2.why: Hitting the origin server + DB for every visitor is expensive and slow. With Data Cache, 1,000 visitors = 1 DB query (until you refresh). It also provides CDN-level speed for data.
pros: DB/API load dramatically reduced.
Response times near-instant.
Surgical invalidation with tags.
cons: Stale data may appear — plan your strategy carefully.
Caching the wrong thing gives all users incorrect data.
Debugging is tough — the answer to "where did the data come from?" is buried in layers.
gotchas: In Next.js 15 the default is no-store — the "fetch is cached by default" shown in 14 tutorials is now incorrect.
Fetches that read cookies/headers are not cached — this is correct for personalized data.
revalidate: 60 does not mean "refresh every 60 seconds" — it means "after 60 seconds, the first request triggers a background refresh".
terms: Server-side persistent cache — stays alive between requests and deployments.
Cache the data (the old default behavior).
Fresh data on every request — do not cache.
where: Blog posts, products, prices — all cache-worthy.
Cart, profile — no-store or cookies-based dynamic rendering.
t1_2.visualCap: First request: miss → origin → saved in cache. All subsequent: hit → instant response.

t1_3.what:
If a route has no dynamic element, Next builds the full HTML at build time and keeps it. Every visitor gets that ready-made HTML from CDNs — the server doesn’t even run.

If any cookies()/headers()/searchParams is used → route becomes dynamic → renders on every request.
t1_3.analogy: Pre-printed pamphlet — printed once at the printing press (build), now distribute 100,000 copies directly. If you need a customized letter (dynamic), you have to write it each time.
t1_3.why: Serving static HTML is the fastest and cheapest — server CPU zero, TTFB near-zero. The goal of Full Route Cache: as many routes as possible stay static, only the necessary parts are dynamic.
pros: Fastest possible delivery — pre-built HTML.
Server cost almost zero for static routes.
SEO perfect — full HTML in the first response.
cons: Build time increases — thousands of routes = longer builds.
Accidentally using a dynamic API makes the route dynamic.
Content updates require revalidation.
gotchas: searchParams usage makes the route dynamic — check the tick/cross symbols in the build output.
Router Cache (client) is a different thing — Full Route Cache is server-side; don’t mix them.
revalidatePath('/blog') invalidates only that route’s cache — the Data Cache is also invalidated if it’s linked.
terms: Static routes’ rendered HTML + RSC payload generated at build time and ready.
If any dynamic API (cookies, searchParams) is used, the route becomes dynamic — it isn’t cached.
revalidatePath/Tag deletes the cached route, so the next request is fresh.
where: Landing, pricing, about — all static, lightning fast.
Posts are static at build, refreshed with revalidate.
Personalized data = dynamic — don’t expect caching here.

t1_4.what:
When you navigate to a route, its RSC payload is saved in the browser memory. If you go back to the same route, there will be no network call — instant navigation.

<Link> prefetches: static routes get the full payload, dynamic routes only the loading skeleton.
t1_4.analogy: Everyday route — you need GPS the first time, then you remember it. Going home to office (back navigation) now reaches without thinking. Prefetch = checking tomorrow’s meeting venue today.
t1_4.why: If a server round-trip occurred on every click, the SPA feel would be lost. Router Cache provides client-side instant navigation — without loading the entire app client bundle.
cons: Stale data can be displayed for up to 30 seconds/5 minutes.
Cache is not visible in DevTools — debugging becomes difficult.
Many Links = many prefetch requests.
gotchas: Router Cache is memory-only — it clears on page refresh.
Prefetch for dynamic routes is only partial (up to the shared layout) — not the full payload.
If a list doesn’t update after a mutation, you probably forgot router.refresh() — a classic bug.
terms: Memory in the browser (client) that stores RSC payloads of visited routes.
The <Link> fetches the route’s payload in advance on viewport/hover.
Requests fresh data for the current route from the server — refreshes the cache.
where: SPA-like smoothness — without the SPA bundle.
Instant — the payload is in the cache.
Sync the UI with server state using router.refresh().
t1_4.visualCap: Prefetch on hover/viewport → instant on click. Completely free from back/forward cache.

t1_5.what:
There are two ways to refresh cached data: time-based ("consider it stale after 60 seconds") and on-demand ("post published? revalidate now").

On-demand is precise — it doesn’t invalidate the entire site, only the related cache.
t1_5.analogy: Milk packet with an expiry date (time-based) — when the date passes, get a new one. And when the shopkeeper says "today’s fresh has arrived" (on-demand) — throw away the old one and take a new one. Both have their own place.
t1_5.why: The problem with only time-based revalidation: if you need to update content immediately, you have to wait up to 60 seconds. With only on-demand: you’d have to write a webhook for every tiny change. Real apps use both.
pros: Fresh when needed, cached when possible — best of both.
Tag-based grouped invalidation — all related items in one shot.
User-facing updates are instant.
cons: You have to remember which tag/path to revalidate.
Wrong tag = cache never invalidates or invalidates the wrong thing.
Can only be called in server context (actions/handlers).
gotchas: revalidateTag invalidates the data cache, but does not invalidate the client’s router cache — you also need router.refresh() for that.
revalidatePath('/') invalidates only the exact / — not everything. For everything use revalidatePath('/', 'layout').
Time-based revalidation is stale-while-revalidate — the first request after expiry still returns the old version.
terms: revalidate: N — after N seconds the cache becomes "stale", and the next request refreshes it.
Attach a tag on fetch, then later invalidate the whole group by that name.
where: Only product pages fresh on stock/price change.
With the action use revalidatePath — UI syncs instantly.
t1_5.visualCap: Time-based: after expiry the first request returns stale data while a background refresh runs. On-demand: refreshes instantly as soon as the publish happens.
